The American Civil War. From eighteen sixty-one to eighteen sixty-five, the deadliest conflict in United States history was fought between the Union in the North and the Confederacy—eleven Southern states that had seceded over slavery and states' rights. Sparked by the election of Abraham Lincoln, the war cost approximately six hundred twenty thousand lives and devastated the South's economy and infrastructure. Though the Union ultimately prevailed, the war's legacy transformed the nation's constitutional structure and left deep scars on race relations that persist today.

The election of Abraham Lincoln in eighteen sixty on a platform of preventing slavery's expansion into new territories prompted eleven Southern states to secede and form the Confederate States of America under Jefferson Davis. The war began at Fort Sumter in April eighteen sixty-one when Confederate forces fired on a federal garrison. First Bull Run in July eighteen sixty-one shattered Northern hopes for a quick victory. The North, despite early defeats and incompetent generals, had decisive advantages: a larger population, industrial capacity, and control of the seas. The South had superior generalship but was economically isolated.

Antietam in September eighteen sixty-two, fought near Sharpsburg, Maryland, was the bloodiest single day in American military history, with twenty-three thousand casualties. Though tactically inconclusive, it halted General Robert E. Lee's first invasion of the North. The Emancipation Proclamation in September eighteen sixty-two, effective January first, eighteen sixty-three, declared slaves in rebel states free. This transformed the war from a battle for the Union into a crusade against slavery and prevented European intervention on behalf of the South. Gettysburg in July eighteen sixty-three, fought in Pennsylvania, became the turning point when Union General George Meade defeated Lee's second invasion. After Gettysburg, the Confederacy was always on the defensive.

General Ulysses S. Grant, made supreme Union commander in eighteen sixty-four, pursued a strategy of attrition and total war, coordinating simultaneous offensives and devastating Confederate resources. Sherman's March to the Sea from eighteen sixty-four to eighteen sixty-five saw Union General William Tecumseh Sherman burn and pillage Georgia and the Carolinas, breaking the South's will to fight. Appomattox Court House in April eighteen sixty-five saw Robert E. Lee surrender to Grant. Within weeks, the other Confederate armies surrendered, ending the war.

The Thirteenth Amendment in eighteen sixty-five abolished slavery throughout the United States. The Fourteenth Amendment in eighteen sixty-eight granted citizenship to all persons born in the country. The Fifteenth Amendment in eighteen seventy forbade racial discrimination in voting. Reconstruction from eighteen sixty-five to eighteen seventy-seven attempted to rebuild the South and integrate formerly enslaved people as citizens, though white Southern resistance, the rise of the Ku Klux Klan, and Northern political weakness eventually reversed many gains. The Civil War was a test of whether a democratic republic could survive internal dissolution and whether a nation founded on the proposition that all men are created equal could abolish slavery. Its scale—over six hundred thousand dead—made it existential. The Union's victory preserved the nation and ended slavery, but Reconstruction's failure left a century-long legacy of racial injustice, segregation, and political disenfranchisement in the South.
